Notes: First Jewish settler: Solomon Pareira, native of Holland, moved to Providence with his wife in 1838 (Foster 1985; notes 'some evidence to suggest earlier Jewish residents' without details).
Solomon Pareira, a Dutch merchant, became the first Jew to settle permanently in Providence.
A minyan met regularly at Solomon Pareira's home, 'perhaps as early as 1844'.
Land on New London Turnpike acquired for a Jewish cemetery, with Pareira as prime mover.
Orthodox group 'Sons of Israel' began gathering for daily services in Providence (origin of Temple Beth-El).
Estimate based on families: by 1850 eight Jewish families had joined the Pareiras (9 families x5); mostly clothing merchants and tailors.
Louis Lewisson, one of the first Jews naturalized in Providence, advertised his clothing business in the Providence City Tax Book in 1852.
First congregation, Sons of Israel, chartered 1854 (per JVL; Foster gives May 1855).
Congregation Sons of Israel received its charter from the Rhode Island General Assembly in May 1855; Pareira first president.
Estimate based on families: eighteen Jewish households at the close of the Civil War.
Estimate based on families: fifty-six Jewish households by 1870, mostly from Germany.
Congregation Sons of David (1871) merged with Sons of Israel (merger printed as '1574', evidently 1874) to form Sons of Israel and David; Sons of Zion founded 1875 in the North End.
Jewish population of the Providence-Pawtucket area had 'almost tripled' since 1870 (no count; combined area).
Approximately 150 Jewish families 'numbering some 500 persons' in Providence AND Pawtucket combined (124 names in city directories); combined two-city figure, not Providence alone.
About 1,000 Jews in Rhode Island (state), 'almost all in Providence and nearby Pawtucket'; state aggregate.
First census of American Jewry tallied Rhode Island (state) Jewish population at 1,000; state aggregate.
Estimate based on families: Providence City Directory for 1880 listed about 125 Jewish family names (editor's note in Segal 1971).

Estimate based on families: Segal concludes about 200 Jewish heads of families in Providence in the 1880s, based on King's Pocket Book of Providence (1882) lodge memberships (B'nai B'rith ~70, Free Sons of Israel ~80).
Estimate based on families: 250 Jewish families in 1885 (other summaries describe these as Jewish names in the city directory).
Estimate based on families: Providence City Directory for 1885 listed about 265 Jewish family names (editor's note).
Estimate based on families: Jewish families increased from 250 (1885) to 992 (1895); mainly eastern European immigrants.
Estimate based on families: number of Jewish families reached 1,607 by 1900 (other summaries describe this as Jewish names in the city directory).

Estimate based on families: 'the thirty-five hundred families of Providence' in the 1905 pogrom-relief canvass; 46 organizations sent delegates. Conflicts with ~8,000 estimates for 1905-1909; families x5 likely overstates. [Review fix: Population ~17500 moved to Notes - families x5 conflicts with ~8,000 for 1905-1909]
'By 1905, there were approximately 8,000 Jews in Providence.'

Jewish Encyclopedia (published 1901-1906; year approximated as 1905): 'growing community in Providence, with four congregations', Associated Hebrew Charities (26 societies), Hebrew Educational Alliance, YMHA. Its 3,500 figure is for Rhode Island state incl. Newport.
Harry Cutler (c.1907) gave the Jewish population of Providence as 'variously estimated as between 7,500 and 10,000' (range; left blank).
Lester Bradner, A Modern City (1909): 'The Jewish population in the city may be reckoned today at 8,000 or 9,000, nearly double what it was five years ago' (range; left blank).
Temple Beth-El built in South Providence in 1911.
Jewish Welfare Board report (1923) estimated the Jewish population of Providence at approximately 14,400 in 1913 (cited by Bernheimer and Kraft).
American Jewish Year Book city table: Providence R.I. Jews estimate 1917-1918.
Jewish Welfare Board report (1923) estimated approximately 16,500 in 1921.
American Jewish Year Book city table: Providence R.I. later Jewish estimate 16,500 (1923).
Linfield, Jewish Population in the United States 1927 (AJYB): Providence 21,000 (7.48% of total 280,600).

Bernheimer and Kraft counted ~2,694 Jewish children aged 6-14 in Providence public schools (1933); a tentative projection of ~17,300 total was not offered as an estimate by the report. Subset/projection; left blank.
AJYB vol. 43 (Linfield) estimate for Providence in 1937; Rhode Island state 27,813.
'In 1937, the Jewish community reached 30,000' - context indicates Rhode Island statewide figure; not city.
Rhode Island state Jewish population peaked at 30,000 in 1937; declined to about 18,000 (state, at time of writing).
General Jewish Committee of Providence formed by 500 delegates from 51 Jewish organizations (May 28, 1945).
AJYB 1948-49 and 1950 figure for Providence of 25,000, based on United Jewish Appeal statistics for 1948.

Group Work and Leisure-Time Needs study (1951): population of Providence proper 15,691 (East Side 6,821; South Providence 5,752; North End 2,696; Downtown 422). Greater Providence total 19,698 (5,934 families).
Third synagogue built on Providence's East Side in 1954.
Goldstein 1963 population survey: 11,023 Jews in 3,638 households (56.7%) lived in the city of Providence proper; Greater Providence almost 19,600.
Greater Providence Jewish population 19,600 by scientific survey, incl. 13,440 in Providence and Pawtucket combined; metro/combined figures.

Goldstein 1970 list-based count: 3,000 Jewish households in city of Providence (5,678 Greater Providence; 6,235 state); households only, probably ~10% undercount, and household size ~3.3 so x5 conversion not applied.
16,000 Jews in Rhode Island, including 14,200 in the Providence area (metro aggregate).
Six congregations in Providence in 2005 (11 elsewhere in the state).
